subsection: 1. The government of Ireland under the Union and the campaign for Catholic Emancipation, 1815–1829

notes.h: The Act of Union and Westminster
notes.b: From 1 January 1801 Ireland was governed directly from London under the Act of Union, which abolished the Irish Parliament in Dublin.
points: The Union joined Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, which came into being on 1 January 1801.
Ireland sent 100 MPs to the House of Commons at Westminster and 28 representative peers to the House of Lords, elected by the Irish peerage.
Four Irish bishops of the Church of Ireland sat in the Lords in rotation, and the Church of Ireland remained the established church.
Legislation for Ireland was made at Westminster, where Irish MPs were a minority of the House of Commons.
Many Irish issues, including tithes and the Catholic question, were debated in a Parliament with a British majority that often showed little interest in them.

notes.b: Authority in Ireland rested with a Lord Lieutenant and a permanent administration in Dublin Castle, answerable to the British cabinet.
points: The Lord Lieutenant was the viceregal head of the executive and was usually a peer appointed by the British government.
The Chief Secretary for Ireland sat in the Commons and was the government's chief minister for Irish business in Parliament.
The Under-Secretary was the senior permanent civil servant, and the Castle administration was known as Dublin Castle.
Grand juries, drawn from the leading landowners of each county, raised local taxes and organised county public works.
Magistrates appointed by the Lord Lieutenant, most of them landowners, handled local justice and policing in the counties.
Local government in the towns was largely in the hands of corporations, many of which were controlled by Protestant oligarchies.

notes.h: Policing and the franchise before Emancipation
notes.b: Security and the vote were both shaped by the Protestant ascendancy of landowners and the Church of Ireland.
points: The Peace Preservation Force was set up in 1814 as a rural police force, and the county constabulary was created in 1822.
The Irish Constabulary was established in 1836 as a centrally controlled force; it later became the Royal Irish Constabulary.
Before 1829 Catholics could vote, provided they held a freehold of at least 40 shillings a year, which gave them the forty-shilling freeholder vote.
Catholics could not sit in the House of Commons, and the oath of supremacy and oath of abjuration excluded them from most public offices.
The veto controversy concerned a proposal that the British government should have a say in the appointment of Catholic bishops in return for Emancipation; the Catholic hierarchy opposed it.

notes.b: The Catholic Association turned the Emancipation question into a mass political movement that could challenge the government at the polls.
points: Daniel O'Connell and Richard Lalor Sheil founded the Catholic Association in Dublin in May 1823 to campaign for Catholic Emancipation.
Membership was open to anyone who paid a subscription of a penny a month, and this made the Association a movement of the ordinary Catholic population.
The Catholic Rent, a collection organised through the parishes and led by the Catholic clergy, raised money for the campaign from 1824 onwards.
The Association's proceedings were widely reported, and it organised meetings and petitions throughout Ireland.
The government suppressed the Association in 1825 under the Unlawful Societies Act, and it was reformed almost at once under a new name.
The clergy were central to the Association, and parish priests collected the Catholic Rent and mobilised voters at the local level.

notes.b: The Clare by-election of 1828 showed that the forty-shilling freeholders would vote as the Association directed, and it forced the government to act.
points: The by-election for County Clare was held in the summer of 1828 after the appointment of William Vesey-FitzGerald as President of the Board of Trade required him to seek re-election.
Daniel O'Connell stood against Vesey-FitzGerald, who had supported Catholic claims in the Commons, and was returned by a large majority.
O'Connell could not take his seat, because the oath of supremacy still applied to him as a Catholic, and he was the first Catholic to be elected for an Irish county.
The result convinced Wellington and Peel that a Catholic MP could be elected in any Irish county and that the Association could not be contained by coercion.
Some historians stress that the Clare result was the decisive moment, while others emphasise the wider pressure of the Association across Ireland over the previous five years.

notes.h: Concession and the Catholic Relief Act, 1829
notes.b: The Wellington–Peel ministry conceded Emancipation to avoid the risk of civil conflict in Ireland.
points: Arthur Wellington, the prime minister, and Robert Peel, the Home Secretary, concluded that Emancipation was needed to prevent serious disorder, and they persuaded the king to accept it.
The Catholic Relief Act received royal assent in April 1829 and allowed Catholics to sit in Parliament and hold most public offices.
Catholics remained excluded from the highest offices of state, including the offices of Lord Chancellor and Lord Lieutenant of Ireland.
The forty-shilling freehold franchise was abolished, and the county franchise was raised to £10, which reduced the Catholic electorate sharply.
British and Protestant reactions included the Brunswick Clubs and Orange Order protests, and Peel's resignation from his Oxford University seat in protest at the concession.
The Relief Act did not address tithes, the established Church, or the disabilities of Protestant dissenters, which left grievances that the later campaigns would take up.

notes.b: O'Connell's record before 1829 explains why he could mobilise Catholic Ireland, and why he was seen as a threat by Protestants and the government.
points: O'Connell was born in 1775 at Carhan, near Cahersiveen in County Kerry, into a Catholic gentry family that had kept its landed position.
He trained as a barrister in Dublin, and his legal practice gave him the public standing that helped him lead the campaign.
He was known as the Liberator because of his role in winning Emancipation, a title that contemporaries used with pride and critics used with irony.
Before 1823 he had campaigned for Catholic relief through the Catholic Committee and the Catholic Board, and he had been involved in earlier protests in the 1810s.
His methods combined constitutional agitation, large public meetings and the threat of mass non-cooperation, but he rejected violence and secret societies.

As a participant he was the central figure in the Association and in the Clare election, and as a witness to Wellington's concession he saw the reversal of the government's position at close quarters.
Contemporary Protestant opinion regarded him as a dangerous demagogue, while many Catholics regarded him as the leader who had brought them into politics.

Later historians have judged his achievement as a decisive step in the growth of Irish mass politics, while noting that the Relief Act was a concession from Westminster rather than a victory of his own making.

keyTerms.definition: The Act of Union of 1800, in force from 1 January 1801, which abolished the Irish Parliament and joined Ireland to Great Britain in the United Kingdom.
The Catholic Relief Act of April 1829, which allowed Catholics to sit in Parliament and hold most public offices.
Hostility and rivalry between religious communities, especially between Catholics and Protestants, which shaped politics, land and public order in this period.
The mass movement founded by O'Connell and Sheil in 1823 to campaign for Emancipation, funded by the Catholic Rent and suppressed in 1825.
A subscription of a penny a month, collected through the parishes from 1824, which funded the Catholic Association's campaign.
A Catholic or Protestant holder of a freehold worth at least 40 shillings a year who had the vote before 1829, abolished as the franchise by the Relief Act.
The dispute over whether the British government should have a say in the appointment of Catholic bishops as a condition of Emancipation.
